report.title: Leaked IAM access key abuse: from repository leak to crypto-mining and S3 theft
report.summary: A CI service IAM access key committed to a public GitHub repo was validated within 11 minutes. The actor enumerated the account, created a backdoor user with admin rights, disabled CloudTrail logging, launched GPU instances for cryptomining in two regions, and bulk-downloaded S3 objects. All subsequent activity pivoted on the new 'backup-svc' user or reactivated disabled keys in a second account.
threat_actors: automated actor (validated key from Tor exit node)

behaviors.description: Actor validated the leaked IAM access key by calling sts:GetCallerIdentity and enumerating account resources including iam:ListUsers, iam:ListAttachedUserPolicies, iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails, s3:ListBuckets, and ec2:DescribeInstances across all regions, originating from a Tor exit node with distinctive aws-cli/1.33.12 Python/3.11.2 Linux/6.1.0-kali user agent.
behaviors.evidence: The first calls came from a Tor exit node (185.220.101.34) with the user agent aws-cli/1.33.12 Python/3.11.2 Linux/6.1.0-kali and were made by the leaked identity arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/ci-deployer: sts:GetCallerIdentity, iam:ListUsers, iam:ListAttachedUserPolicies, iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails, s3:ListBuckets, ec2:DescribeInstances (every region).

behaviors.description: Actor created a new IAM user 'backup-svc' and attached the full AdministratorAccess policy, then created an access key and login profile to establish persistent console access, pivoting all subsequent activity to this backdoor account.

observables.note: Creation of access key for backdoor user
Console password set for backdoor user

behaviors.evidence: The actor created a new user and gave it full administrative rights: iam:CreateUser userName=backup-svc, iam:CreateAccessKey userName=backup-svc, iam:AttachUserPolicy userName=backup-svc policyArn=arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess, iam:CreateLoginProfile userName=backup-svc (console password set).

behaviors.description: Actor disabled CloudTrail organization trail and deleted the trail in us-east-1, and deleted the GuardDuty detector in the same region to reduce visibility of malicious activity.
behaviors.evidence: In us-east-1 the actor stopped and later deleted the organisation trail: cloudtrail:StopLogging name=org-trail, cloudtrail:DeleteTrail name=org-trail. It also called guardduty:DeleteDetector in the same region.

behaviors.description: Actor launched GPU-accelerated p4d.24xlarge EC2 instances in ap-south-1 and sa-east-1 (regions the organisation had never used) with user data installing XMRig cryptominer, using ec2:RunInstances, ec2:CreateKeyPair, and ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress with 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22.
behaviors.evidence: Within an hour the actor launched sixteen p4d.24xlarge instances in ap-south-1 and sa-east-1, regions the organisation had never used, each with user data that installed XMRig: ec2:RunInstances instanceType=p4d.24xlarge count=8 (ap-south-1), ec2:RunInstances instanceType=p4d.24xlarge count=8 (sa-east-1).

behaviors.description: Actor listed and downloaded objects from bucket acme-customer-exports using s3:ListObjectsV2 followed by thousands of s3:GetObject calls over 40 minutes, exfiltrating 23 GB total from a Tor exit node, after previously setting a bucket policy to grant public read access (which was denied by SCP).

observables.note: Attempt to grant public read access

behaviors.evidence: The actor listed and downloaded objects from the bucket acme-customer-exports using s3:ListObjectsV2 followed by thousands of s3:GetObject calls over 40 minutes, 23 GB in total, all from the Tor exit node. The bucket had previously only been read by the DataPipelineRole role from inside the VPC. The actor also called s3:PutBucketPolicy on the bucket to grant Principal: "*" read access.

behaviors.description: Actor reactivated a disabled IAM access key of an existing user in a second victim account and attached AdministratorAccess via iam:AttachRolePolicy to assume administrative privileges from that account.
behaviors.evidence: In a second victim account the actor instead called iam:UpdateAccessKey to reactivate a disabled key of an existing user and iam:AttachRolePolicy to add AdministratorAccess to a role it could assume.

candidates.title: IAM AttachUserPolicy AdministratorAccess To User backup-svc
candidates.rationale: Attaching the AWS-managed AdministratorAccess policy to a newly created user named 'backup-svc' is a precise, high-confidence indicator of backdoor account creation. The policy ARN is constant and the username appears only in this intrusion, making the pair durable and low-noise.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate admins occasionally attach AdministratorAccess to break-glass users, but the username 'backup-svc' is unique to this campaign. Rule requires both the exact policy ARN and the username to appear together in one AttachUserPolicy event.

candidates.title: CloudTrail DeleteTrail org-trail And GuardDuty DeleteDetector
candidates.rationale: Deleting the organization-wide CloudTrail trail named 'org-trail' and deleting a GuardDuty detector in the same region are deliberate defense-evasion actions never performed by normal ops. Each is a single API call; the trail name is environment-specific but the DeleteTrail event itself is extremely rare.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Trail deletion can occur during CloudTrail reconfiguration, but it is always paired with CreateTrail/UpdateTrail in the same session. Rule keys on DeleteTrail without a preceding CreateTrail from the same identity within a short window (handled by SOC enrichment). GuardDuty DeleteDetector has no legitimate automated equivalent.

candidates.title: EC2 RunInstances p4d.24xlarge In Unused Regions
candidates.rationale: The p4d.24xlarge instance type is GPU-accelerated and exclusively used for cryptomining in this report. The organisation had never used ap-south-1 or sa-east-1. A single RunInstances event with this instance type in a previously unused region is a strong, single-event indicator.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate GPU workloads could launch p4d instances, but only in approved regions. Rule should be enriched with a reference set of authorised regions; alerts on regions outside that set are high-fidelity.

candidates.title: S3 GetObject Bulk Download From Tor Exit Node
candidates.rationale: Thousands of GetObject calls from a Tor exit node with the distinctive kali user agent over 40 minutes exfiltrated 23 GB. While volume requires counting, a single GetObject from a known Tor IP with that user agent is already anomalous for a bucket previously accessed only by a VPC role.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Tor exit nodes rotate; maintain a feed of current Tor IPs. The kali user agent (aws-cli/1.33.12 Python/3.11.2 Linux/6.1.0-kali) is highly specific to the actor. Legitimate clients never use this UA from Tor.

candidates.title: IAM UpdateAccessKey Reactivation With AttachRolePolicy AdministratorAccess
candidates.rationale: Reactivating a disabled access key (UpdateAccessKey status=Active) and attaching AdministratorAccess to an assumable role in a second account shows credential theft and privilege escalation. Each is a distinct event; UpdateAccessKey reactivation is the rarer single-event signal.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Admins occasionally rotate keys, but reactivating a previously disabled key (status from Inactive to Active) without a concurrent CreateAccessKey is unusual. Pair with source IP / user agent mismatch to the key's normal operator.

skipped: B1: Initial validation/enumeration calls (sts:GetCallerIdentity, iam:ListUsers, etc.) are observable but the Tor IP and user agent are already covered by D4/D5; the enumeration APIs are too common to be distinctive single-event detectors.
plan.notes: All rules target AWS CloudTrail events (product:aws, service:cloudtrail). Fields used: eventName, requestParameters.*, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, userAgent. Rules are single-event; enrichment (authorised regions, Tor IP feeds, known-good user agents) is expected at the SOC layer. Priority ordered by specificity and centrality to the intrusion.

history.summary: 7 evasion variants -> positives 7/7, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/90

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P7 represent realistic operator tooling (CLI, Console, SDK, CloudShell) and source diversity while preserving the exact rule selection fields verbatim. They demonstrate that a well-written rule keyed on the four selection fields will catch the attack across common AWS client surfaces. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign look-alikes: attaching the same policy to a different user, attaching a different policy to the target user, and an automated inventory process; none match all four selection fields simultaneously, so the rule stays specific. Out-of-scope evasions O1-O3 are realistic attacker adaptations that the current exact-match rule misses: O1 varies policy ARN casing (IAM vs iam) which the API accepts and CloudTrail records verbatim; O2 substitutes a customer-managed policy clone with identical effect, requiring policy-content analysis to catch; O3 achieves the same privilege grant via group policy attachment (AttachGroupPolicy) followed by AddUserToGroup, a different eventName not covered by this rule. These are reported for analyst awareness; the rule would need loosening (case-insensitive ARN matching, policy equivalence logic, or multi-event correlation) to catch them, which may increase noise.

rules.redteam_analysis: The rule is a precise three-way conjunction (Tor exit IP + GetObject event + Kali user-agent substring). Positive variants P4–P8 show surface changes that a well-written rule still catches: extra wrapper text around the user-agent (prefix/suffix), different buckets, different identity types (IAM user vs assumed-role), extra request parameters, and different Tor IPs from the static list. All keep the three selection literals verbatim. Negative variants N1–N3 are benign look-alikes that share the user agent but originate from clean corporate, pentest, or CI/CD IPs — they must not match. Out-of-scope variants OOS1–OOS4 represent realistic evasions the current logsource and rule structure fundamentally cannot see: unlisted Tor exit nodes, upgraded tooling that alters the user-agent fingerprint, a precursor ListObjectsV2 call, and pivoting through a compromised cloud host. Covering OOS1 requires a dynamic Tor-IP feed or broader reputation enrichment; OOS2 needs a more resilient Kali fingerprint (e.g., regex on 'Linux/.*kali'); OOS3/OOS4 demand behavioural chaining or VPC-flow analysis beyond a single-event rule.

rules.redteam_analysis: The rule is narrowly scoped to four exact field matches (eventName, eventSource, instanceType, awsRegion). Negative variants N1-N3 show benign activity that must not trigger: same instance type in authorized regions (us-east-1, eu-west-1), different GPU type in unauthorized region (g5.24xlarge), and autoscaling automation in authorized region. title: IAM Access Key Reactivation From Disabled State

description: Detects reactivation of a previously disabled IAM access key (status changed from Inactive to Active) which may

rules.author_notes: The rule focuses on the rare event of reactivating a disabled key (status transition from Inactive to Active) without a concurrent CreateAccessKey, which reduces noise from legitimate key rotation workflows. The filter excludes CreateAccessKey events to avoid flagging standard key rotation where a new key is created and the old one is deleted.
rules.redteam_analysis: The rule triggers on UpdateAccessKey with status=Active, which is the only API for reactivation. Evasion variants P4-P8 show realistic operator variations: different identity types (assumed-role, root, federated), SDKs (CLI, Go, Java, .NET, Console), source IPs (IPv6, cloud, Tor), regions, and session contexts. All preserve the required fields (eventName, requestParameters.status) so a well-written literal-match rule catches them. Negative variants N1-N3 represent authorized reactivations (admin maintenance, automated DR, owner recovery) that match the rule but are benign; they demonstrate the need for enrichment (tags, source IP, identity) to reduce false positives. Out-of-scope variants OOS1-OOS3 achieve the attacker's goal (credential access, privilege escalation) via different APIs (CreateAccessKey, AssumeRole, UpdateLoginProfile) that this rule's logsource and fields cannot see; they require separate detection logic.
